Measured content

Does the vial hold what the label says?

Purity and quantity are different questions. A sample can be almost entirely the right peptide and still be a few milligrams light.

The laboratory weighs the peptide content of each lot, and this summary compares that measurement with the strength printed on the label, averaged across every lot where both numbers exist.

Three measurements

The three questions each report answers

  1. HPLC

    How clean is it?

    Liquid chromatography splits the sample into its components. The main peak’s share of the total signal is reported as percent purity — a relative figure, not a weight.

  2. MS

    Is it the right molecule?

    Mass spectrometry weighs the molecule itself. The result is compared against the mass calculated from the compound’s sequence or formula to confirm identity.

  3. QUANT

    How much is there?

    A quantitation run reports the milligrams of peptide actually recovered from the vial, which is the number printed next to “of label” in the table.

Random spot checks

Extra screening on lots picked at random

On top of the three measurements every report carries, we send randomly chosen lots for further screening: heavy metals, sterility and bacterial endotoxin. Most lots are never screened. When one is, the result appears on that lot’s report page exactly as the lab wrote it; when one isn’t, the page shows nothing for it rather than suggest a test that never ran.

  • METALS

    Any metal contamination?

    Trace metals can enter during synthesis, drying or handling. The screen reports arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury one element at a time, and the result goes on the lot it was run on, whatever it shows.

  • STERILITY

    Does anything grow?

    A sample from the vial is cultured to see whether anything grows. The result covers the tested lot only, and it does not mean the material is suitable for use in people or animals.

  • ENDOTOXIN

    How much endotoxin?

    Measures bacterial endotoxin in the material, given in endotoxin units (EU) exactly as the lab prints it.

Reading the table

What one row tells you

The card is the most recently reported lot, pulled straight from the table. Start with the lot code: if it matches your label, the rest of the row describes the material in your vial.

Read purity and content as a pair. The first is a percentage of what the instrument detected; the second is a weight compared with the label. Neither one stands in for the other.

Where the lab runs a public lookup, the outbound link lets you see the same result on their site rather than taking ours on trust.
